narrative:
The model estimated a 58.7% probability that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. In practical terms, it judged failure more likely than passing, and that is why your application was denied. Your gender and race were not used in this prediction.

The denial was driven mainly by your class-rank position in the third year, which was the strongest factor and pushed the prediction toward failure. A third-year decile of 2 is far below the average of about 5.79 among accepted students, signaling substantially weaker recent academic performance. Your first-year decile of 1 was the second most influential factor and also pushed toward failure; it is similarly far below the accepted-student average of about 6.00. Your law school admission test score was the third most important factor, and it pushed in the opposite direction, toward passing. At 36 it is only slightly below the accepted-student average of about 37.18, so it helped your case but was not enough to overcome the two class-rank signals.

To improve a future application, focus on the factors that can be strengthened: retake the admission test if you can improve your score, consider additional academic work or a post-baccalaureate program to demonstrate readiness, and seek pre-law or admissions advising. Ask the school for feedback, apply to programs with holistic review, and explain any context that affected your grades in a personal statement.
